\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

All numbers in this section come from one cached run of every path on every query
(8,150 validation questions from DocVQA and InfographicVQA over 1,786 page images) on a single
GeForce RTX 4090 (Table~\ref{tab:hardware}). Costs are measured, not priced: GPU-seconds, energy from NVML, and wall-clock
latency per query. Routers are trained and evaluated on 5 page-grouped 60/20/20 splits, so no page
appears in more than one split; each test split holds 1,548--1,653 questions. Unless marked
otherwise, policy results are means ($\pm$ standard deviation) over the 5 seeds; figures marked
``seed 1'' show the first split.


\subsection{Cost and answer quality of each path}
\label{sec:res-paths}

All three paths use the same generator (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, greedy decoding). The text path reads the top-3
BM25 pages of OCR text; the visual path reads the top-1 ColPali page image (at most 1280 visual
tokens); the hybrid path reads both. Over all 8,150 questions, always-text reaches ANLS 0.367 at
0.43 GPU-s per query, always-visual 0.546 at 0.62 GPU-s, and always-hybrid
0.570 at 1.01 GPU-s (329\,J).
With a shared local generator the text path is therefore \emph{not} a cheap path:
OCR text costs about as many input tokens as a page image, and the text path is much less accurate.
The real cost differences are between one context and two (hybrid costs 1.6$\times$ the visual path and
2.3$\times$ the text path) and the size of the visual index at scale (Section~\ref{sec:res-scale}).
In 35\% of queries every path fails. For 76\% of these, no path had the gold page in its
context (page recall@1 is 0.44 for BM25 and 0.57 for ColPali; Table~\ref{tab:retrieval}). No router
can recover these queries; they bound every policy.

Two controls on 1,500 of these questions (750 per dataset; Table~\ref{tab:controls}) show where the
differences between paths come from. First, the visual advantage is a matter of modality, not of how many pages
the generator reads: at equal depth, one page image beats one page of OCR text by 0.22 ANLS (95\% interval
0.194, 0.247), and three page images beat the three-page text path by 0.22 (0.189, 0.245), whereas going
from one page to three adds only 0.041 for text and 0.038 for images. Second, retrieval errors cost more
than any choice of path. Given the gold page, the visual path rises from 0.544 to 0.826, the text path
from 0.364 to 0.604 and the hybrid path from 0.556 to 0.839; the gain is largest on DocVQA
(+0.42 for the visual path, against +0.14 on InfographicVQA). Even with the gold page, the
image beats its OCR text by 0.22 ANLS (0.16 on DocVQA, 0.28 on InfographicVQA), and
adding the OCR text to the gold image adds only 0.013 (0.000, 0.024). Three page images reach ANLS
0.582, above the hybrid path, but take 3.3$\times$ the generation time of one image; such a path is
outside the evaluated path set.

\subsection{Outcome-based route labels}
\label{sec:res-labels}

Route labels are derived from measured outcomes: the label of a query is the path that maximises
$\mathrm{ANLS} - \lambda \cdot \mathrm{cost}$, with ties broken towards the cheaper path (Table~\ref{tab:labels}).
Labels from a keyword rule over the question text agree with these outcome labels on 68.5\% of queries,
with Cohen's $\kappa = 0.01$, i.e.\ no agreement beyond chance; the keyword rule sends 97\% of
queries to the text path. On the 5,275 queries that at least one path answers, agreement falls to
52.7\% ($\kappa = 0.005$): most of the overall agreement comes from queries that every path
fails, which tie and default to the cheaper text path. Routing accuracy measured against keyword labels therefore says nothing about cost or answer
quality.

\subsection{Routing policies}
\label{sec:res-policies}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} compares fixed policies, a keyword rule, simple learned baselines,
CAVR, the content-aware CAVR-CE and the per-query oracle. All router costs include the router's own measured
overhead and, where the router reads ColPali scores, ColPali retrieval for every query.

CAVR on question embeddings alone (ANLS 0.542 $\pm$ 0.014) shows no significant difference from always-visual:
on every seed the 95\% bootstrap interval of the ANLS difference includes zero and lies within
$\pm$0.007, while CAVR uses 4\% more GPU. The question text alone does not predict
which path will succeed.
CAVR-CE adds what is available before generation: an mpnet cross-encoder reads the question with the
best-matching OCR passages of the retrieved pages, plus retrieval scores and ColPali per-token match statistics.
With $\lambda$ chosen on each seed's validation split (the cheapest $\lambda$ within 0.005 ANLS of always-hybrid),
CAVR-CE reaches ANLS 0.557 $\pm$ 0.015 at 0.716 GPU-s per query, against
0.566 $\pm$ 0.020 at 1.009 GPU-s for always-hybrid: 29\% less GPU compute
(25--36\% across seeds; Table~\ref{tab:router_ce_tests}).
The price is a small ANLS loss: CAVR-CE is lower than always-hybrid on 4 of 5 seeds
(mean difference $-0.008$, range $-0.015$ to $+0.001$), and the 95\% bootstrap interval
excludes zero on 2 of 5 seeds. On exact match, McNemar's test finds no significant difference
on 5 of 5 seeds ($p = 0.098$--$0.74$), but with only 80--107
discordant pairs per seed it is underpowered, so this does not show that the two policies are equivalent.
Against always-visual, CAVR-CE gains $+0.012$ to $+0.018$ ANLS (bootstrap interval above zero on
5 of 5 seeds; McNemar on exact match $p \le 0.029$ on 5 of 5 seeds)
for 15\% more GPU.
Part of the saving over always-hybrid comes from using the hybrid path less often, whichever queries are chosen.
A quality-blind random mix of always-visual and always-hybrid at CAVR-CE's GPU cost reaches ANLS 0.547
(in expectation, computed per seed), and at CAVR-CE's ANLS it costs 0.896 GPU-s. The saving attributable
to choosing queries is therefore 20\% (13--26\% across seeds), or $+0.010$
ANLS at equal cost.

The per-query oracle reaches ANLS 0.630 $\pm$ 0.016 at only 0.486 GPU-s, so substantial headroom
remains. It is limited by prediction: CAVR-CE predicts per-path success with a mean AUC of 0.842
(0.839 for gradient boosting on the same tabular features), and a learning curve over 25--100\% of the
training pages (2 seeds) rises only from 0.826 to 0.841.

\subsection{Runtime budget control}
\label{sec:res-lambda}

The decision rule $\arg\max_p \hat{q}_p - \lambda c_p$ takes the cost weight $\lambda$ at serving time, so one
trained router covers a range of budgets without retraining. Sweeping $\lambda$ from 1 to 0 moves CAVR-CE from
ANLS 0.502 at 0.56 GPU-s to 0.564 at 0.84 GPU-s (mean over seeds;
Figure~\ref{fig:pareto} shows seed 1). Table~\ref{tab:load_test_ops} gives the serving capacity of each operating
point on seed 1.

  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/pareto.png}
  \caption{Cost--quality frontier of each router as $\lambda$ is swept (seed 1), with fixed policies and the
  per-query oracle. Costs are measured GPU-seconds per query including router overhead.}

\subsection{Confidence-based escalation}
\label{sec:res-escalation}

Escalation sends a query to the hybrid path when a calibrated probability that its routed answer is good falls
below $\tau$ (Table~\ref{tab:escalation}, Figure~\ref{fig:escalation}). Probabilities are calibrated on the
validation split by logistic regression; their expected calibration error on test is 0.027--0.078
depending on the signal. On top of CAVR-CE, re-routing on the ColPali score margin at $\tau = 0.5$ raises ANLS
from 0.557 to 0.564 and GPU cost from 0.716 to 0.856 GPU-s
(34\% of queries escalated), still 15\% below always-hybrid.
Setting $\lambda = 0$ reaches the same point without escalation (ANLS 0.564 at 0.845 GPU-s), and
the signal and $\tau$ shown here were highlighted after inspecting test results, so this comparison is exploratory.
Because the re-routing decision is made before generation, it adds no serial step, and its latency cost is small:
p95 latency rises from 1.24\,s to 1.36\,s, against 1.39\,s for always-hybrid. Signals
that judge the generated answer (token log-probabilities) can be computed only after the routed answer exists. Computed from the measured
per-stage times, a serial cascade has p95 1.91\,s; launching the hybrid path alongside the routed path cuts
p95 to 1.42\,s but costs 1.46 GPU-s per query, 45\% more than always-hybrid (assuming two
concurrent workers).

\subsection{Scalability, throughput and energy}
\label{sec:res-scale}

\paragraph{Serving under load.} A Poisson load test with dynamic batching, simulated from the measured per-query
service times and measured batching curves, gives the highest arrival rate one GPU sustains at p95 $\le$ 2\,s and
the number of GPUs needed for a given load (Table~\ref{tab:load_test}, mean over seeds; Figure~\ref{fig:gpus},
seed 1). Serving 100 queries/s at p95 $\le$ 2\,s needs 106.0 $\pm$ 0.7 GPUs for always-hybrid,
72.4 $\pm$ 4.4 for CAVR-CE (32\% fewer), 64.4 $\pm$ 0.5 for always-visual and
41.6 $\pm$ 0.9 for the oracle. At this target batches rarely form: the ratio of GPUs needed by CAVR-CE and always-hybrid (0.68)
tracks their ratio of batch-1 GPU-seconds (0.71). The saving depends on the target, as the sweep below shows. With HF Transformers
generation (no serving engine such as vLLM~\cite{vllm}), one GPU serves at most 3.88 (text), 3.06
(visual) and 1.80 (hybrid) queries/s at the best batch size within memory. The simulation keeps the
evaluation index (1,786 pages) on every GPU; routing saves generation compute, not index memory, because
CAVR-CE reads ColPali scores for every query.
Across p95 targets from 1.5 to 10\,s, on all five splits, CAVR-CE needs 22--32\%
fewer GPUs than always-hybrid and 10--16\% more than always-visual (Table~\ref{tab:slo_sweep}).
The simulator charges a batch the mean generation time of its members, scaled by the measured batching curve;
charging the longest member instead, a conservative bound, the saving over always-hybrid is 30\% at 2\,s and
15\% at 5\,s (against 24\% with the mean member).

\paragraph{Generation and retrieval together.} The load test keeps the small evaluation index on every GPU. For a
large corpus, a retrieval tier is needed as well. Projected from the workstation's measured MaxSim throughput at
batch 64, scaled linearly in pages and at full utilisation, 100 queries/s over a million pages needs 20 GPUs
for retrieval (14 just to hold the index) for every policy that reads ColPali on every query. CAVR-CE then
needs 92 GPUs in total, against 126 for always-hybrid and 84 for always-visual. The question-only
router could skip ColPali for the queries it sends to the text path, but it sends only 2\% there and
needs 84 GPUs. Routing thus saves the same number of generation GPUs at any corpus size, while the index
adds a cost that every visual policy pays.

\paragraph{Load-adaptive $\lambda$.} On a fixed pool of 74 GPUs, the number CAVR-CE needs for 100 queries/s
at p95 $\le$ 2\,s, arrivals alternate between 80 queries/s for 60\,s and 140 queries/s for
20\,s (split 1). CAVR-CE at its validation-chosen $\lambda$ answers 77.5\% of requests within 2\,s
(ANLS 0.560); always-hybrid manages 34.8\%. A controller that raises $\lambda$ when the oldest
queued request has waited longer than a threshold (chosen on validation queries) moves 18\% of requests to a
higher $\lambda$ and reaches 80.1\% (ANLS 0.559), whereas a fixed $\lambda = 0.2$ reaches
88.3\% (ANLS 0.551) and always-visual 88.7\%. In this simulator overload appears mostly as
larger and slower batches rather than long queues, so a queue-driven controller reacts little; adapting $\lambda$
to load needs a better overload signal, such as GPU busy time, which we leave open.

\paragraph{Visual index scaling.} ColPali stores 1,031 vectors per page. At 100k pages the index needs
24.6\,GiB in bf16, more than our 24\,GiB GPU holds before any model weights or activations, and a
million pages (about 246\,GiB) would exceed the memory of most current accelerators
(Table~\ref{tab:index_scaling}, Figure~\ref{fig:index}). Streaming it from pinned host memory costs
1,044\,ms per query; 2$\times$2 pooling shrinks it to 6.3\,GiB and 10.3\,ms
but lowers recall@1 on the real corpus from 0.577 to 0.525 (both measured with the same batched
query encoding). Hierarchical token pooling~\cite{tokenpooling}, which clusters each page's patch vectors and keeps
one mean vector per cluster, does much better at the same size: with 263 vectors per page it keeps recall@1 at 0.574 and recall@5 at
0.747, against 0.578 and 0.751 for the full index and 0.525 and 0.712 for 2$\times$2
pooling (Table~\ref{tab:token_pooling}). A 3.9$\times$ smaller index makes a million pages 63\,GiB,
which 5 A10s could hold, and scoring cost falls in proportion to the vectors per page. Emulated sharding over
2 GPUs (shards timed one after another on this GPU) gives
19.8\,ms. A GPU-resident index answers in 0.55\,ms at 1k pages and 19.8\,ms at
50k pages.

\paragraph{Offline cost.} Building a 100k-page index would take about 1.7 GPU-hours, extrapolated from a 64-page
benchmark at batch 4 (16.2 pages/s); the 1,786-page evaluation index was built at batch
8, which exceeded GPU memory, and ran at 11.3 pages per GPU-second. docTR OCR of the
1,786 evaluation pages took 471\,s and 29.3\,kJ.

\paragraph{Multi-GPU index sharding.} On the three-GPU node (Table~\ref{tab:multi_gpu},
Figure~\ref{fig:multi_gpu}), sharded search returned the same top page as one GPU for all 500 check questions
(99.8\% exactly, the rest exact score ties). Latency is set by the number of pages per GPU. A 50k-page index is
searched in 327\,ms on one GPU, 164\,ms on two and 109\,ms on three (speedup
2.99$\times$); from 50k pages up, parallel efficiency is at least 99.6\% and dispatch and merge
add at most 0.6\,ms over an ideal split. Throughput at batch 64 scales by the same factor, with
efficiency of at least 99.7\% from 10k pages up. With 50k pages per GPU, a
150k-page index of 36.9\,GiB, larger than the memory of any one GPU on the node, is searched in
328\,ms, as fast as 50k pages on one GPU (weak-scaling efficiency 99.9\%). Smaller
corpora gain less at batch 1 (three GPUs give 2.51$\times$ at 1k pages and 2.52$\times$ at 10k pages),
where per-query overheads are a larger share of a short search; their batch-64 throughput still reaches
96\% and 102\% of linear scaling.

Energy per query for the whole node falls from
28.4\,J on one GPU to 17.8\,J on three at 50k pages, but not because the GPUs work more efficiently: an
unused GPU, which holds a CUDA context in the benchmark process, draws about 51\,W (estimated from the runs; 50--53\,W across
configurations), and without the idle draw the active energy is 17.8\,J per query whatever the number of GPUs.
On a node whose GPUs are powered anyway, spreading the shards over all of them therefore lowers the energy per query.
These GPUs are much slower than the workstation's: one Tesla P40 takes 327\,ms for the 50k-page search that
the RTX 4090 completes in 19.8\,ms in bf16, 17$\times$ faster. Absolute times therefore do not
transfer between the machines; the scaling with the number of GPUs does. It also shows that the emulated sharding above
omitted little: merging the shard results costs well under a millisecond.

\paragraph{Sharding on data-centre GPUs.} The same benchmark, unchanged, ran on a node with two
NVIDIA A10 GPUs (Ampere, scored in fp16; Table~\ref{tab:hardware_multigpu}). Sharded search again returned the same
top page as one GPU for all 500 check questions (99.8\% exactly, the rest exact score ties). A
50k-page index is searched in 41.1\,ms on one A10 and 21.0\,ms on two (parallel efficiency
97.6\%); from 50k pages up, dispatch and merge add at most 0.5\,ms, and batch-64
throughput efficiency is at least 98.6\% from 10k pages up. A 100k-page index
(24.6\,GiB, more than one A10 holds) is searched in 41.4\,ms on two GPUs, as fast as
50k pages on one (weak-scaling efficiency 99.2\%), and the largest corpus run on two A10s,
120k pages, took 49.5\,ms. One A10 is 8$\times$ faster than one P40 on the 50k-page search and uses
5.6$\times$ less active energy per query (3.2 against 17.8\,J), largely because it
scores in fp16 on tensor cores, which the P40 lacks; it is still 2.1$\times$ slower than the RTX 4090.
As on the P40 node, active energy per query does not depend on the number of GPUs (3.2 and
3.2\,J at 50k pages). Near-linear sharding therefore holds across two GPU generations and two scoring
precisions; the parallel efficiency transfers between machines, the absolute speed does not.

\paragraph{Host-memory placement at a million pages.} With the index held in host memory, two NVIDIA A10 GPUs
searched a million pages (246\,GiB). Held in GPU memory within the same 70\% per-GPU budget
(15.6\,GiB), this index would need 16 A10s, or 8 nodes like this one
(Table~\ref{tab:host_stream}, Figure~\ref{fig:host_stream}). Streamed search returned the same top page, up to the
repetition of real pages in the corpus, and the same score as GPU-resident search for all 100 check questions
on 100k pages. Single queries were bound by the PCIe link: their latency stayed within 4\% of
the time needed to copy each GPU's shard, and at a million pages it was 10.9\,s on one GPU and
6.4\,s on two. The workstation shows the same bound, streaming 100k pages from host memory in
1,044\,ms against 1.10\,s on one A10. One A10 read host memory at 24.2\,GB/s and two
together at 41.0\,GB/s, 85\% of twice the single-GPU rate, so a second GPU cut single-query latency by
only 1.7$\times$. The cause of this shortfall was not identified: nvidia-smi reports a path through several PCIe
bridges between the two GPUs, and the placement of host memory across the two CPU sockets was not controlled.

Batching removes the PCIe bound, because one pass over the index serves every query in the batch. Scoring rather than
copying sets the pace from about 25--30 queries per batch, a crossover derived from the batch-1 and
batch-64 times on the assumption that scoring time grows linearly with batch size. At batch 64 and
a million pages, throughput was 2.25 queries/s on one GPU and 4.50 on two (2.0$\times$),
or 0.44\,GPU-s per query; GPU-resident search would cost about 0.43\,GPU-s, scaled linearly from
its 100k-page run. Where both placements were measured on the same corpus (100k pages, two GPUs),
streamed search reached 94\% of the GPU-resident throughput at batch 64 with a GPU energy of
6.7 against 6.4\,J per query; the host CPU and memory energy that streaming adds was not measured.
At batch 1 the comparison reverses: streamed search used 1.29 against 0.083\,GPU-s and
99 against 15\,J per query. Host-memory placement therefore trades latency for GPU count at about
the same throughput per GPU, but only for workloads that fill large batches. At 6.4\,s per single query and
about 14\,s per batch of 64, it misses the 2\,s p95 target of the load test and suits batch or offline
search. Interactive search over a million pages needs GPU-resident sharding, projected at about
51\,ms on 16 A10s (linear fit of the resident runs against pages per GPU, without the cost of
merging results across nodes), or a compressed index.

\paragraph{Router overhead.} The CAVR router (mpnet embedding and MLP) takes 11.7\,ms per query at
batch 1 on the GPU (25.0\,ms on the CPU) and reaches 12,454 queries/s at large
batch. CAVR-CE takes 24.8\,ms and 1.74\,J per query at batch 1, and its cross-encoder sustains
389 queries/s. Neither is a bottleneck next to generation (Table~\ref{tab:router_throughput}).

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:res-limits}

All measurements except index sharding and the host-memory index use one consumer GPU (GeForce RTX 4090) under Windows; caps on visual tokens and OCR length keep memory
below the point where the driver spills to system RAM. Generation uses HF Transformers rather than a serving
engine such as vLLM~\cite{vllm}, so absolute capacity is pessimistic; the comparison between policies is the main
result. The 2\,s latency target is our choice; the saving is smaller at looser targets.

The load test is a simulation driven by measured service times, not live traffic, and escalation latencies are
computed from measured per-stage times rather than measured on concurrent workers. The simulator assumes an ideal
global queue and unlimited CPU, charges a batch the mean generation time of its members (the longest-member bound is reported), and keeps the
1,786-page evaluation index on every GPU, so the retrieval tier for a large corpus is projected rather than simulated. Costs
are measured without prefix or encoder caching, which would favour paths whose page image repeats across
questions. Indexes of 10k--1M pages
repeat the real page embeddings, which is valid for latency and memory but not for retrieval quality at that
scale; the recall of pooled indexes is measured on the 1,786 real pages only. Multi-GPU sharding was measured for retrieval only, on two server nodes with at most three GPUs
each (Tesla P40, NVIDIA A10), whose absolute times do not transfer to the workstation, and the load test does not include sharded retrieval. The host-memory index was measured in one process on one node, with 5 latency queries and 2
repetitions per batch (latency varied by at most 0.5\% within the run) and with host memory placed across CPU
sockets without control, and GPU-resident search at a million pages is
projected from smaller resident runs, not measured.

Energy covers the GPU only (NVML); host CPU and memory energy is not counted. Answers are short (at most
32 tokens), so cost is dominated by processing the input; with longer answers the relative cost of an
extra context shrinks. The savings are relative to this path set and one shared generator, and they depend on the
retrieval depth and input caps of each path (the depth controls cover 1,500 questions and one more depth per
modality); routing to a smaller generator was not tested. The router handles text
queries over visual documents; queries that contain an image are out of scope. The router design was developed on the same five splits that we
report on, and the feasibility analyses that motivated it looked at their test portions; no parameter of the final
pipeline is selected on test data, but a held-out confirmation set would give a cleaner estimate. Splits group
questions by page, so pages of one DocVQA document can fall into different splits. Finally, the 35\% of
queries that every path fails bound what routing can achieve on this benchmark.
